title: Make the conversation experience feel settled
recap: Eleventh item built: a conversation with unread opens on the first unread line and holds it. Waiting on the gap number and the arrival.

field_values.brief:
Khushal wants the conversation experience to stop feeling worse than the chat products he uses. This Ticket owns the parts where the answer is a judgement about how it should look and move. A separate Ticket owns the defects where there is nothing to draw, and it is named at the end so you can tell them apart.

Four changes are agreed with him and are not open for you to re-decide. You may propose how they look; you may not propose that they are unnecessary.

**One. The steered label goes.** When a turn settles, a message can carry a chip reading "steered" or "sent now". It comes from `modeChip` in `web/src/components/conversation/ConversationTranscript.svelte`. Steering is the default, so the label tells him what he already assumes, and when a message is genuinely refused he is told separately. Remove the distinction rather than restyle it.

**Two. The dead band above the input is too tall.** It should be very small. It is not one value. `.chat-thread` in `assets/app.css` carries a bottom mask that fades the last 16px, the thread's own bottom padding is `var(--space-4)`, and `NEWEST_LINE_BOTTOM_GAP_PIXELS` in `web/src/components/conversation/viewport/viewportConfiguration.ts` keeps another 24px under the newest line. Decide the total, say which of the three carries it, and show the result at the top and bottom both, since the top fade is a different number again.

**Three. Typing in the peeked view must not eat the conversation.** Today a growing draft takes its room from the thread above it. It should grow the peeked view instead. The peeked view is 60% of the page, set on `.conversation-layer:has([data-conversation-state="peeked"])` in `assets/app.css`. Decide how far it may grow and what happens when it reaches that.

**Four. A sent message is drawn once and never moves.** Press Enter and the browser draws the message itself at the end of the thread. Then the record comes back and decides where it really belongs: a steer joins the turn already running rather than starting one, so the message lands above where he just saw it, and a refused steer that gets queued moves out of the thread entirely and up above the composer. See `outgoingMessagesByPlace` in `web/src/lib/conversation/outgoing.ts` and the stack in `web/src/components/conversation/composer/HeldPromptStack.svelte`. The target: it appears at the end, stays there, and does not change appearance. How it was delivered does not get to decide where it sits. If delivery genuinely fails, that is said where the message already is rather than by relocating it. Your job is what that looks like while its fate is unknown, and what failure looks like in place.

**And the thing that runs through all four: motion.** He finds the experience jittery. The target is smooth and functional, not animated — no bouncing, no over-easing, minimal jumping about. This is a goal of the work and not a finish applied at the end. You cannot judge it from a still picture, so you have to live in the thing.

## What you must do before you draw

Use the product. Open a conversation, send messages, watch what happens to them, scroll, switch between focus and full, resize, type a long draft in each state. The jitter is the point; find where it comes from rather than taking his word for where.

Then use your own HTML the same way. A wireframe that is only looked at proves nothing about motion.

Then go and use conversation experiences that are better than ours. ChatGPT does not need an account. Claude, T3 Chat and open-source chat components are all readable. Bring back what specifically makes them feel settled, not a list of features.

## Two artifacts

The first does only the four changes above and the motion target. Nothing else in it.

The second holds anything further you believe moves us towards how ChatGPT or Claude feel. Everything in it must be marked as yours rather than his, and each item must say what it costs and what it risks. He will decide on that one separately. Do not mix the two.

## Out of bounds

The focus and full split is not in question. You may change things around it; you may not change the concept.

The composer itself is out of bounds except for the one change named above. Its max height is being fixed in the other Ticket and is not yours.

The overall structure of the peeked view and the larger prompt box is not in question.

## Things that are already true, so do not draw them as problems

Focus mode shows his own messages, messages explicitly addressed to him, permission asks and answers, and turns that ended badly. It does not show ordinary agent output at all. It is already the narrow view.

In focus mode, messages addressed to him currently collapse behind the turn head. That is being removed in the other Ticket — a message addressed to him will never fold again. Draw focus mode with no fold in it.

Scrolling back through a long conversation hits a wall and judders. That is a measured defect in the conversation loading work, with its own Ticket. It is not yours to design around, and it will go away without you. Do not claim it.

## Handoff

Whatever reaches an implementer has to carry the four agreed changes and the motion target as an explicit list, marked as agreed with Khushal, separately from anything you added. The point of the split is that the split survives the handoff.

The defects live in the Ticket titled "Repair the conversation defects behind the composer and the fold". Do not do its work.

## Eleven. Where a conversation opens when something is unread

Added by Khushal after the wireframe was filed, so this one is new work rather than a reduction.

Opening a conversation that has something he has not read puts him at the very bottom, which is
the wrong place: the thing he opened it for is above him. His guess, and it is a good one, is that
it should open with the top of the view aligned to the start of the most recently unread message,
and that the top line should be held as the pane expands from peeked to opened rather than the
bottom being held.

The fact that makes this buildable, so you do not design around a constraint that is not there:
the read position already exists and is durable. `owner_read_through_sequence` is stored per
conversation server-side, advanced through its own `owner-read` endpoint, published in the
conversation record, and already read by the client in `wire.ts`. So the first unread message is
knowable without inventing any new state.

What the design has to answer:

- Nothing unread. Presumably today's behaviour, the newest line. Say so rather than leave it.
- The unread run is taller than the view. Top-aligning the first unread is right, but say what he
  sees and where the eye is meant to go.
- The first unread message sits above what is loaded. The reader keeps its mounted window on the
  newest rows, so this costs a page fetch backwards. Say what he sees while that happens, because
  the honest answer may be that opening is no longer instant in that case.
- A new message arrives mid-expansion. Decide whether the held top line survives it.

The constraint to respect rather than fight: the existing anchoring is real and tuned —
`NEAR_NEWEST_LINE_PIXELS`, `SENT_MESSAGE_TOP_GAP_PIXELS`, `NEWEST_LINE_BOTTOM_GAP_PIXELS` and
`MOST_HELD_LINES` in `viewport/viewportConfiguration.ts`, and a reader whose mounted window is
pinned to the newest rows. A rule that top-aligns an older line while something else is holding
the newest one will fight itself. Say which holds in which case.

pending_proposal.body:
One artifact: [how it moves](/files/tickets/t_02zd37tz/artifacts/wireframe-smooth.html). Two things to watch in it.

The four you settled are settled and not drawn again: 12px under the newest line, one number where today there are three, the same peeked and opened; a draft grows the peeked view, not the thread; a sent message is drawn once, goes to the top, and never moves again — what comes back fills in beneath it, and once that space is used the newest line is the bottom of the view; failure is said in place; the card travels between states in 150ms; one centred pill; a conversation with something unread opens on the first unread, held 12px down; and no tool call in Focus at any point. One test decides the lot: is the newest line in the view.

*An answer arriving.* Three causes sat behind the judder. Two are not judgement calls and are settled there. The fade was tied to scroll position, so arriving words landed under it; a fade means there is more below you have not seen, and arriving text is not that — so it is gone while you are at the bottom. And the glide used the product's ease, which spends a third of its distance in the first frame and then crawls. It is an even curve over 240ms. The third is yours: once the free space under your message is spent, the view can snap to the end as today, move a line at a time, or rise. Fastest frame 26px, 15px, 4px. Try them on Bursty; a steady answer flatters all three. I would take a line at a time.

*A message waiting.* The queue is yours already and drawn as it is — its inset, its five rows before it scrolls, every rule the app's, bar the serif, which would have been the only serif on this page. What was never drawn is how a message gets in and out of it, and that is one gesture, not three: a thing rises out of the top of the input box. A message you send rises out of it into the conversation. A message the composer will not send rises out of it as a row. A message you send from the queue rises out of it again. **The one change to what happens today: a message that cannot steer never enters the thread at all, where today it is drawn at the end and then relocates.**

Two things you will meet that are already true today. Opening marks the whole delivered run read, not the part you looked at, so a tall unread run lands you at the first unread once and at the end next time. And holding an unread line at the top needs room kept under it, which scrolling up eats a pixel at a time and never gives back.

Still unanswered: you said the input caps at six lines and the sixth should grow to four. The cap is built; the four I do not follow.
